n: The high priest asks Stephen whether the charges against him are true. What follows is the longest speech in Acts — a survey of Israel’s history showing that God was never confined to one place and that Israel often rejected his messengers.
Stephen addresses the council respectfully as brothers and fathers. He begins with Abraham: the glorious God appeared to him in Mesopotamia — outside the Holy Land, long before any temple.

f.w: The God of glory appeared unto our father Abraham

f.g: Haran, a city in northern Mesopotamia.

n: God called Abraham to leave his land and relatives and go to a land God would show him.

f.w: Get thee out of thy country

n: Abraham left the land of the Chaldeans, settled in Haran, and after his father’s death God moved him into the land of Canaan where they now live.

f.g: The book of Abraham adds that his father Terah stayed in Haran and returned to idolatry.

n: God gave Abraham no land there — not even a foot’s length — yet promised it to him and his descendants, when he didn’t even have a child. Abraham lived by faith in promises.

f.w: not so much as to set his foot on
when as yet he had no child

n: God told Abraham his descendants would be foreigners in another land, enslaved and mistreated for about four hundred years.

f.g: entreat = treat; mistreat them.

n: God would judge the nation that enslaved them, and afterward they would come out and worship him in this place.
God gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision. Abraham fathered Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day; Isaac fathered Jacob, and Jacob the twelve patriarchs.
The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt — but God was with him. Stephen’s first example of Israel rejecting the one God chose to save them.
God rescued him from all his troubles, gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, and Pharaoh made him ruler over Egypt and the royal household.
A famine struck Egypt and Canaan, and their ancestors could find no food.

f.g: dearth = famine, scarcity.
Canaan.

n: Hearing there was grain in Egypt, Jacob sent his sons there the first time.

f.g: corn = grain, such as wheat or barley.

n: On their second visit Joseph revealed himself to his brothers, and Pharaoh learned about Joseph’s family. Like Jesus, the rejected brother is recognized the second time.

f.w: at the second time Joseph was made known

n: Joseph sent for his father Jacob and all his relatives — seventy-five people in all.

f.g: 75 people. Stephen follows the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew text of Genesis 46:27 gives 70, counting differently.

n: Jacob went down to Egypt, where he and the patriarchs died.

Their bodies were brought back to Shechem and buried in a tomb bought from the sons of Hamor. Stephen compresses several burial traditions; Genesis records Abraham buying a cave at Hebron and Jacob buying land at Shechem.

f.g: Shechem, in the region later called Samaria.

n: As the time approached for God to fulfill his promise to Abraham, the Israelites grew greatly in number in Egypt.

f.w: the people grew and multiplied in Egypt

n: Then a new king came to power who did not know about Joseph.

f.w: another king arose, which knew not Joseph

n: He schemed against their people and oppressed them, forcing them to abandon their infants so they would die.

f.g: subtilly = craftily, with cunning.

n: At that time Moses was born, a beautiful child in God’s sight, and was cared for at home for three months.

f.g: Literally “beautiful to God” — favored by God.

n: When he was set out, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and raised him as her own son.
Moses was educated in all the learning of Egypt and was powerful in words and deeds.

f.w: learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians
f.g: Egypt was renowned for learning in writing, mathematics, astronomy, and medicine.
Moses later felt slow of speech, but his words carried power.

n: At forty, he decided to visit his fellow Israelites.

f.g: Jewish tradition divided Moses’s 120 years into three periods of forty: Egypt, Midian, and the wilderness.

n: Seeing an Israelite being mistreated, he defended him and struck down the Egyptian.
Moses assumed his people would realize God was using him to deliver them — but they didn’t. Again, God’s chosen deliverer is misunderstood.
The next day he tried to make peace between two quarreling Israelites, reminding them they were brothers.

f.w: would have set them at one again
f.g: Tried to reconcile them, make them “at one” — the root idea of “atonement.”
strove = fought, quarreled.

n: But the man in the wrong pushed Moses away: “Who made you ruler and judge over us?”

f.w: Who made thee a ruler and a judge over us?

n: “Are you going to kill me like you killed the Egyptian yesterday?”

f.g: diddest = did.

n: At this Moses fled and lived as a foreigner in Midian, where he had two sons.

f.g: Midian, a region east of the Gulf of Aqaba.

n: Forty years later, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the flames of a burning bush in the wilderness near Mount Sinai — once more, God revealing himself far from any temple.

f.w: a flame of fire in a bush

f.g: Sinai.

n: Amazed, Moses went closer to look, and the Lord’s voice spoke to him.
The Lord declared himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses trembled and didn’t dare look.

f.w: I am the God of thy fathers

n: The Lord told him to take off his sandals, because the place where he stood was holy ground. Holiness comes from God’s presence, even in a desert.

f.w: the place where thou standest is holy ground

n: God had seen his people’s suffering and heard their groaning, and had come down to rescue them; he would send Moses to Egypt.

f.w: I have seen, I have seen the affliction of my people

n: Stephen drives the point home: the very Moses the people rejected — “Who made you ruler and judge?” — God sent as ruler and redeemer. The parallel to Jesus is unmistakable.

f.g: The Greek word for deliverer here is lytrōtēs — “redeemer,” a word that points to Christ.

n: Moses led them out, performing wonders in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years.
This same Moses foretold that God would raise up a prophet like him from among them — the Messiah. Rejecting Jesus means rejecting Moses’s own words.

f.w: A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you

n: Moses was with the congregation in the wilderness, with the angel at Sinai and with their ancestors, and received living words to pass on to them.

f.g: “Church” here means the assembly or congregation of Israel.
lively oracles = living words, revelations from God.

n: But their ancestors refused to obey him, pushed him aside, and in their hearts longed to go back to Egypt.

f.w: in their hearts turned back again into Egypt

n: They told Aaron to make them gods to lead them, since they didn’t know what had happened to Moses on the mountain.

f.w: Make us gods to go before us

f.g: wot = know.

n: They made a calf idol, sacrificed to it, and celebrated what their own hands had made — preferring a god they could build and control.

f.w: the works of their own hands

n: So God let them go their way, to worship the stars. Stephen quotes Amos: during forty years in the wilderness, were their sacrifices truly offered to God?

f.g: Sun, moon, and stars worshipped as gods.

f.w: as it is written in the book of the prophets

n: Instead they carried shrines of pagan gods like Moloch and the star-god Rephan, so God would exile them beyond Babylon.

f.g: A Canaanite god associated with child sacrifice.
The Greek Old Testament’s form of a star-god name (Hebrew Kiyyun), perhaps Saturn.
Amos says “beyond Damascus”; Stephen updates it to the Babylonian exile that actually happened.

n: Stephen turns to the sanctuary: their ancestors had the tabernacle of testimony in the wilderness, built exactly as God showed Moses. A portable sanctuary — God moved with his people.

f.g: fashion = pattern, design.

n: The next generation brought it into the land with Joshua when God drove out the nations, and it remained until David’s time.

f.g: Here “Jesus” is the Greek form of Joshua, Moses’s successor — not Jesus Christ.
drave = drove.

n: David found favor with God and asked to build a dwelling place for the God of Jacob.

f.w: desired to find a tabernacle for the God of Jacob

n: But it was Solomon who built God a house.
Yet the Most High does not live in buildings made by human hands. Stephen isn’t against temples; he is against confining God to one.

f.w: the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands

n: He quotes Isaiah: heaven is God’s throne and earth his footstool — what house could anyone build for him?

f.w: Heaven is my throne, and earth is my footstool

n: “Didn’t my hand make all these things?”

f.w: Hath not my hand made all these things?

n: Then Stephen turns his history lesson into a direct indictment: they are stubborn and closed in heart and ears, always resisting the Holy Ghost, just like their ancestors.

f.g: Like an ox that will not bend its neck to the yoke.

n: Which prophet did their fathers not persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One — and now they have betrayed and murdered him.

f.w: Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted?

n: They received the law delivered by angels, yet failed to keep it — the very law they accuse Stephen of attacking.

f.g: disposition = arrangement, administration.

n: Enraged and cut to the heart, the council grinds their teeth at him.

f.w: gnashed on him with their teeth
f.g: gnash = grind the teeth in fury.

n: Full of the Holy Ghost, Stephen gazes into heaven and sees God’s glory and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. He sees two distinct beings — the Father and the Son.

f.w: saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God

n: He announces that the heavens are open and he sees the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand. Elsewhere Jesus is pictured seated; here he stands — perhaps rising to receive or vindicate his faithful witness.

f.w: the Son of man standing on the right hand of God

n: They shout, cover their ears, and rush at him together.
They drag him out of the city and stone him. The witnesses lay their outer cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul — the future apostle Paul.

f.w: cast him out of the city

n: As the stones fall, Stephen prays, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” — echoing Jesus’s own words on the cross, now addressed to Jesus himself.
Kneeling, he cries out, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them,” and with that he dies — “falls asleep.” Like his Master, he forgives his killers. He is the first Christian martyr.

f.w: Lord, lay not this sin to their charge
